item.title: [NH] NH Education Daily — Hot Off the Press: The Ballot Decisions That Will Reshape NH School Districts
item.description:
A one-hour breaking special, October 13, 2026: Three weeks before November 3, every NH voter faces Question 2 — the HB 1300 school tax cap. Alex and Jordan unpack what the ballot says vs. what RSA 32:5-i actually does, Londonderry's warning of million in cuts, district-by-district impacts from Hudson to Oyster River to Mascenic, the failed court challenges, and what real voters are posting on social media right now — verified posts from both sides. Plus: what a levy cap means for special education's unfunded mandates.

item.title: [NH] NH Education Deep Dive — Who's Teaching Special Ed? NH's Staffing Shortage
item.description:
The NH Fiscal Policy Institute's new report projects 1,114 teacher openings a year through 2034, with staffing down 5.7%, the pipeline halved, and teachers earning a third less than comparable professionals. Alex and Jordan unpack what it means for special education — endorsement barriers, the para crisis, the contracting trap, FAPE risk — and what districts can actually do about it.

item.title: [NH] NH Education Deep Dive — The Burden Shift: How HB 581 Rewrote the Rules of Special Ed Disputes in New Hampshire
item.description:
In 2021, New Hampshire moved the burden of proof in special education due process hearings off of parents and onto school districts. Alex and Jordan break down HB 581 — what changed, what it means for parents and districts, and what it demands of NH special education teams in their daily work. Educational guidance, not legal advice.
Work with our consultant One-on-one help for parents from an NH special education administrator: IEP reviews, meeting prep, Prior Written Notice — what to ask for, and how to ask for it. Consults $250 — book a consult: [link]
Sources - HB 581 as introduced (2021), full bill text (PDF), NH General Court archives: https://gencourt.state.nh.us/BillHistory/SofS_Archives/2021/house/HB581H.pdf - RSA 186-C:16-b, current text — Due Process Hearing; Appeal (see paragraph III-a), official NH General Court statute site: https://www.GenCourt.state.nh.us/rsa/html/XV/186-C/186-C-mrg.htm - "NH Changes Law Regarding Burden of Proof in Special Education Due Process Hearings," Disability Rights Center–New Hampshire, Aug 2, 2021: https://drcnh.org/statements/burden-of-proof-in-due-process-hearings/ - "Sununu signs bill shifting burden of proof in special education hearings to schools," Keene Sentinel (via NH Bulletin), 2021: https://www.keenesentinel.com/news/local/sununu-signs-bill-shifting-burden-of-proof-in-special-education-hearings-to-schools/article_78864d50-12bb-5eac-8d49-78cb31042cbf.html - NH Department of Education, FY26 "Rules and Laws in Excess" chart (PDF): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/fy26-nh-rules-and-laws-in-excess-chart.pdf - 2025 Compilation of Education Legislation, NH School Boards Association (PDF) — includes HB 754 (automatic discovery): https://nhsba.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/2025-Compilation-of-Ed-Legislation-for-2025-Legislative-Summary.pdf - "New Hampshire Shifted the Due Process Burden to Schools in IEP Disputes. Sixty-three uses of force by Omaha-area school resource officers since 2021 — including shock gloves used on a special education student, force concentrated with a few officers, and a majority of incidents involving Black students who are about 15 percent of enrollment — examined in full, with Nebraska's LB 390 memorandum law, Rule 51 manifestation and behavior-plan protections, and federal IDEA and Section 504 guidance, plus concrete takeaways for families, IEP teams, and school boards.
Sources: - Flatwater Free Press, "School resource officers in Omaha-area schools have used force on students dozens of times since '21" (Oct 20, 2026): https://flatwaterfreepress.org/school-resource-officers-in-omaha-area-schools-have-used-force-on-students-dozens-of-times-since-21/ - Associated Press via SRN News, "Nebraska's largest school district asks police to stop using electric shock gloves on students" (Aug 20, 2026): https://srnnews.com/omahas-largest-public-school-district-stops-officers-from-using-electric-shock-gloves/ - Education Rights Counsel summary of Lincoln Journal Star seclusion investigation (Aug 2026): https://www.educationrightscounsel.org/news/nebraska-schools-force-kids-into-seclusion-rooms-we-dont-know-how-often-its-happening — verify by searching the Lincoln Journal Star site for "seclusion rooms" and the reporter name Livia Ziskey, August 4, 2026. - Nebraska Revised Statute 79-2704 (memorandum of understanding contents, LB 390 of 2019): https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/statutes.php?statute=79-2704 — verify by searching nebraskalegislature.gov for "79-2704". - Unicameral Update, "Best practices adopted for school resource officers" (LB 390 passage, 48-0): https://update.legislature.ne.gov/?p=25962 - Rule 51, 92 NAC 51 (incl. 016.02 manifestation determination, FBA/BIP, 45-day interim alternative setting): https://www.esu5.org/sites/default/files/ck_upload/Rule%2051_May_2022.pdf - Nebraska Department of Education, Guidance Document: Supporting the Behavioral Needs of Children with Disabilities: https://www.education.ne.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Supporting-the-Behavioral-Needs_2025-1.pdf - Nebraska Department of Education news release, Nebraska Meets Requirements under IDEA Part B and Part C for 2026 (June 23, 2026): search education.ne.gov News Releases for "Nebraska Receives Highest IDEA Determination" / "Meets Requirements". - U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights guidance on restraint and seclusion of students with disabilities and OCR/OSERS guidance on disciplining students with disabilities: verify by searching ed.gov / aasa.org for "OCR, OSERS Release New Guidance on Disciplining Students With Disabilities" and "Restraint and Seclusion of Students with Disabilities" Dear Colleague guidance. - item.title: [Connecticut] Education Daily — October 21, 2026: Build It at Home — In-District Special Education Grants and the Apprenticeship Pipeline
item.description:

item.title: [New Jersey] Deep Dive — 210 Hours Owed: The Hillside Case and the Last Mile of Enforcement
item.description:
Five months after the New Jersey Department of Education found Hillside Public Schools failed to deliver a student's IEP services and ordered 210 hours of make-up instruction plus 45 hours of therapies, the parent says she still has no compensatory plan — this deep dive traces the case from the September 2025 placement loss through the October 15 compliance review, explains how New Jersey's state complaint and corrective action system works, and separates a clean data submission from actually delivered services.
Sources: - NJ21st, Oct. 15, 2026, NJDOE Found Hillside Failed a Student With Disabilities. Five Months Later, What's Been Fixed? (May 6, 2026 NJDOE report and corrective action plan in complaint C2026-7612, timeline, deadlines, and October status): https://nj21st.com/2026/10/15/njdoe-found-hillside-failed-a-student-five-months-later-whats-been-fixed/ - NJ21st, Oct. 2, 2026, NJ DOE Responds to Holmdel Report: Why District Responses Aren't Shared with Parents (NJDOE spokesperson Mike Yaple's written explanation of the one-year correction rule, complaint files, monitoring, and final determinations): https://nj21st.com/2026/10/02/nj-doe-responds-to-holmdel-report-why-district-responses-arent-shared-with-parents/ - NJDOE broadcast memo, Sept. 30, 2026, Required: Complete NJSLEDS Fall Submissions by October 15 (special education practice period closes Oct. 15; complaints should not be the only route to compensatory services): https://sites.ed.gov/idea/?p=84731 To verify without a stable URL: search nj.gov for "N.J.A.C. 6A:14-9.2 complaint investigation" to read the full complaint rule text (one-year lookback, 60-day investigation, 15-day error notice); item.title: [New Hampshire] Deep Dive — State Complaints, ESY, and Compensatory Education
item.description:
This deep dive walks through the three dispute tools that meet in one file folder: the state complaint under 34 CFR 300.151 through 300.153 and New Hampshire's Ed 1121 process (who can file, the sixty-day clock, the commissioner's signed decision, the twenty-day reconsideration rule, and the public complaint summaries required by RSA 186-C:5-a); extended school year under 34 CFR 300.106 and New Hampshire's Ed 1110.01 (individual team determination, the regression and recoupment standard, and the factors beyond regression); and compensatory education under the qualitative "but for" standard of Reid v. District of Columbia, 401 F.3d 516 (D.C. Cir. 2005), including the First Circuit's Pihl decision and real New Hampshire complaint orders that required districts to deliver compensatory services. The episode closes with the documentation habits that decide these cases in practice. Plain-English explanations of the governing rules, with settled law distinguished from practical interpretation, for working New Hampshire special education teachers and case managers.
### Sources
- 34 CFR 300.151–300.153 (state complaint procedures, remedies, and filing contents): https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/34/300.152 — also search eCFR at ecfr.gov for "300.151 adoption of State complaint procedures" and "300.153 complaint contents" to read the adopted text of all three sections side by side. - New Hampshire Rules for the Education of Children with Disabilities, Ed 1121 (complaint process) and Ed 1110.01 (extended school year): full rule text at https://www.gc.nh.gov/rules/state_agencies/ed1100.html — find Ed 1121 in Part Ed 1121 and Ed 1110.01 in Part Ed 1110 on that page; annotated copy with cross-references in the Guide to the NH Standards for the Education of Children with Disabilities at https://picnh.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Guide-to-the-NH-Standards-3.1.2024.pdf - NH Department of Education, Special Education State Complaint Process flow chart (sufficiency triage, investigation, commissioner's decision, corrective action): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/flow-chart-special-education-complaint-process.pdf - NH Special Education Procedural Safeguards Handbook (complaint steps, sixty-day decision, twenty-day reconsideration, corrective action during reconsideration): https://core-docs.s3.amazonaws.com/documents/asset/uploaded_file/163/District/2787706/NH_Special_Education_Procedural_Safeguards_Handbook.pdf - RSA 186-C:5-a (state complaint tracking system and required public posting of redacted complaint summaries): https://law.justia.com/codes/new-hampshire/title-xv/chapter-186-c/section-186-c-5-a/ - NH Department of Education, Special Education State Complaint #25-35 (corrective action plan ordering the team to determine missed progress and implement compensatory services): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/case-25-35.pdf - NH Department of Education, Special Education Complaint 22-04 (late-start speech and language services during the extended school year period): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/case-22-04.pdf - Reid ex rel. Reid v. District of Columbia, 401 F.3d 516 (D.C. Cir. 2005) (qualitative compensatory education standard): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/401/516/551622/ - Pihl v. Massachusetts Department of Education, 9 F.3d 184 (1st Cir. 1993) (compensatory education available after eligibility ends): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/9/184/540521/ - OSEP, "Return to School Roadmap: Development and Implementation of Individualized Education Programs in the Least Restrictive Environment under the IDEA" (Sept. 30, 2021), Question E-2 (a child may receive both ESY and compensatory services): https://sites.ed.gov/idea/idea-files/return-to-school-roadmap-development-and-implementation-of-ieps/ - 34 CFR 300.106 (extended school year services): search eCFR at ecfr.gov for "300.106 extended school year services" to read the full regulation text, including the prohibitions on limiting ESY by disability category or by type, amount, or duration. - Disability Rights Center–NH, "Filing a Special Education Complaint" (plain-language walkthrough of the NH investigation and decision process): https://drcnh.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/SPED_File_Complaint.pdf

item.title: The Plan Nobody Audits: Section 504's Quiet Quadrupling
item.description:
This deep dive examines the fastest-growing accommodation system in American public schools: plans under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 held by students who do not have IEPs. Drawing on the U.S. Department of Education's Civil Rights Data Collection for 2023–24 and the leading published research, Alex and Jordan walk through what a Section 504 plan is and how its three-part eligibility test differs from the IDEA; how the "504-only" rate climbed from 1.1% of students in 2009–10 to 3.9% in 2021–22 and about 1.9 million students (4%) in 2023–24; why rates range from near double the national average in Texas and New Hampshire to below half in New Mexico and Mississippi, with individual Texas middle schools above 30% and other schools at zero; the documented skew toward White students (60% of 504-only students against 44% of enrollment) and, in the first study to link school records to IRS tax data, toward higher-income families (2.9% vs. 1.5%), even as IEPs run the opposite way; the measured response of 504 enrollment to the College Board's 2017 decision to honor school accommodations on the SAT automatically; the costs of both over-identification and under-identification; and the central evidentiary gap — no national breakdown of 504 plans by condition and no national audit of 504 eligibility has ever been published, so claims about how many plans are "unnecessary" exceed what the evidence can support. Plain-English explanations, with every number sourced and the limits of the evidence stated on air.
### Sources
- U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, "A First Look: The Civil Rights Data Collection, 2023–24" (September 2026) — 19% of students with disabilities (15% IDEA; 4% / ~1.9M Section 504 only); White students 60% of 504-only vs. 44% of enrollment; boys 56% of 504-only: https://www.ed.gov/media/document/2023-24-first-look-civil-rights-data-collection-september-30-2026-114593.pdf - Perry A. Zirkel, "Concerns About Misidentification of '504-Only' Students," ATPE News, March 30, 2026 — 1.1% (2009–10) to 3.9% (2021–22); Texas 7.6%; 23 of the top 25 districts (14.4%–17.4%); Texas middle schools at 23.1%–30.1%; three-part eligibility test; no federal/state funding; costs of over- and under-identification; Texas dyslexia analysis: https://atpenews.org/concerns-about-misidentification-of-504-only-students/ - Perry A. Zirkel, "Mis-identifying '504-Only' Students," eSchool News, February 6, 2026 — New Hampshire and Texas at almost double the national rate; New Mexico and Mississippi at less than half; California 2.1% with districts ranging 0%–13.9% and schools 0%–24.2%: https://www.eschoolnews.com/innovative-teaching/2026/02/06/mis-identifying-504-only-students/ - Zirkel et al., analysis of the 2009–10 Civil Rights Data Collection, Journal of Disability Policy Studies (2014), reported by Education Week — 504-only rates: White 1.26%, Black 0.57%, Hispanic 0.50%; Title I schools 0.84% vs. non-Title I 1.23%: https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/students-with-504-plans-more-likely-to-be-white-enrolled-in-non-title-i-schools/2014/08 - Holler & Zirkel, national survey of Section 504-only students (2008), reported by Education Week — mid-2000s rate of about 1.2%; ADHD the most commonly listed impairment, diabetes next: https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/counting-section-504-students/2008/03 - Ainsworth et al., Oregon study linking school records (2008–09 to 2018–19) to IRS tax data (paper released January 2026), and Tiffany Liu, study of 504 enrollment after the College Board's 2017 SAT accommodation policy (March 2026), both reported by The 74 / Disability Scoop, June 9, 2026 — 504 receipt 2.9% near the top of the income distribution vs. 1.5% near the bottom; IEP receipt about 25% among the most disadvantaged; verbatim comments from Nick Ainsworth, Paul Morgan, Ben Lovett, Miriam Nunberg, and Christopher Cleveland: https://www.disabilityscoop.com/2026/06/09/wealthy-students-more-likely-to-get-disability-accommodations-study-finds/32038/ - Tiffany Liu's College Board finding as also reported by Education Daly — the 504 enrollment response about 24% larger in the most affluent communities than in high-poverty schools: https://www.educationdaly.us/p/we-need-to-talk-about-504-plans - U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, "Dear Colleague Letter and Resource Guide on Students with ADHD" (July 26, 2016) — districts must not assume that strong academic performance rules out a substantial limitation in a major life activity: https://www.wrightslaw.com/law/memos/ocr/sec504.adhd.2016.pdf - Disability Scoop, "Nearly 1 In 5 Public School Students Have IEPs Or 504 Plans" (October 19, 2026) — the 19% total is up from 17% in the prior (2021–22) collection: https://www.disabilityscoop.com/2026/10/19/nearly-1-in-5-public-school-students-have-ieps-or-504-plans/32226/

item.title: The List Nobody Can See: Inside the Child Care Food Program's Seven-Year Blacklist
item.description:
One routine Federal Register notice this fall renewed the paperwork behind the National Disqualified List — the Child and Adult Care Food Program's national bar on institutions, sponsoring organizations, day care home providers, and the individuals who run them. This deep dive opens up the machine: how a review finding becomes a "serious deficiency," how the corrective-action clock runs, why quitting does not save you, the appeal you get — and the six decisions 7 CFR 226.6(k)(3) says you can never appeal — and how a listing lasts seven years, or longer if a program debt is unpaid. Plus the vagueness problem the National CACFP Association put in writing (the same citation can mean a serious management problem in one state or "three small errors on a reimbursement claims form" in another), the patchwork early-removal door, the Feeding Our Future record that explains why the list exists, and the 2024 proposed rule (FNS-2024-0005) that would rebuild the process — still unfinalized. USDA does not publish the list or its size; where the public record runs out, this episode says so.
Sources: - 7 CFR 226.6 (CACFP State agency responsibilities — serious deficiency process at (c), National Disqualified List at (c)(7), administrative review at (k), day care home reviews at (l)): https://www.casemine.com/regulation/us/640f05fa8b0a3c5be33657ac/amp (also available at eCFR, Title 7, Part 226, §226.6) - USDA Food and Nutrition Service, "Proposed Rule: Serious Deficiency Process in the CACFP and SFSP" (docket FNS-2024-0005; comments due May 21, 2024; page updated February 4, 2026): https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/cn/fr-022124 - Proposed rule as published, 89 FR 13150 (February 21, 2024): https://www.cacfp.org/assets/pdf/SD+Propsoed+Rule+FR+Document+2024-02108/ - National CACFP Association (National CACFP Sponsors Association), comment letter on FNS-2024-0005, May 17, 2024 (signed Lisa Mack, President & CEO): https://files.constantcontact.com/e5582ed6201/f25b5196-65c4-4976-9cad-8cd96d1c625c.pdf - National CACFP Association, "NCA Response – National Disqualified List Information Collection," August 5, 2026: https://www.cacfp.org/2026/08/05/nca-response-national-disqualified-list-information-collection/ - National CACFP Association, Quarterly Policy Update, October 2026 (NDL information-collection comment summary): https://www.cacfp.org/2026/10/07/quarterly-policy-update-october-2026/ - USDA Food and Nutrition Service, "Why CACFP Is Important" (program scale and authority): https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/cacfp/why-cacfp-important - item.title: [Wyoming] Education Daily — October 23, 2026: One Definition of Reading Proficient
item.description:
Wyoming reopens its K-12 language and literacy rules today: the Notice of Intent goes to the Governor on October 23, stakeholders have asked for a state-defined definition of grade-level reading proficiency and a fixed list of approved screeners and materials, and a new 45-day comment period will follow — while screening under the 2026 Wyoming Language and Literacy Act continues this fall and eight districts pilot home literacy packs for grades 1-2.

item.title: [Maine] Education Trends — Chronic Absenteeism: One in Four Students, and the Long Climb Back
item.description:
One in four Maine students is chronically absent — the rate fell from a 31.1 percent pandemic peak to about 24 percent and then stalled — and this hour examines who is missing school, why, what five million lost instructional hours cost, and the Maine responses with results behind them, from the Maine Engagement and Attendance Center and early warning systems to Maine Indian Education's drop from the fifties to 19.6 percent.
Sources: Maine Department of Education, Data Warehouse — Chronic Absenteeism (definition: enrolled at least 10 days, missed 10% or more of days enrolled, excused or unexcused) and Enrollment: https://www.maine.gov/doe/data-reporting/reporting/warehouse/visualizations Maine Department of Education, Maine's Model of School Support (chronic absenteeism as an accountability indicator): https://www.maine.gov/doe/Testing_Accountability/model Maine Engagement and Attendance Center (MEAC, established 2024; national Attendance Works figures cited there: 28% national rate in 2022-23, 30% peak, 16% in 2018-19; Maine 31% in 2021-22, 27% in 2022-23, 24% in 2023-24): https://www11.maine.gov/doe/index.php/meac Maine KIDS COUNT Data Center, Chronic Absenteeism (24.4% in 2024-25; 40,980 students; economically disadvantaged 34.5% vs 15.7% for higher-income students): https://datacenter.aecf.org/data/tables/10836-chronic-absenteeism?loc=21&loct=2 Maine Education Association, How Count ME In! is Tackling Chronic Absenteeism Across Maine (24.1% / nearly 41,000 students in 2023-24; peak 31.1% / 53,265 in 2021-22; 16.5% in 2017-18; 5,000,000 instructional hours lost in 2023-24; Jess Anderson quote; teacher-call timing at 1-3 and 4-6 days): https://maineea.org/maineeducatoronline/how-count-me-in-is-tackling-chronic-absenteeism-across-maine/ Count ME In!, For Families (barriers: transportation, work schedules, caregiving, housing, long distances, weather, rural access; support-focused documentation steps): https://www.countmeinmaine.org/for-families Maine DOE Newsroom, Maine Engagement and Attendance Center Continues Bringing Statewide Partners Together (June 17 meeting; MEAC partners Count ME In! and Maine PBIS; proactive root-cause mission): https://mainedoenews.net/2026/09/04/maine-engagement-and-attendance-center-continues-bringing-statewide-partners-together-to-strengthen-student-attendance/ Bureau of Indian Education, Maine Indian Education Posts Landmark Gains in Attendance and Achievement (systemwide 19.6% in 2024-25; Indian Island School 13.1%; Sipayik Elementary 18.7%; Indian Township School 27.0%; Maine statewide ~24%): https://www.bie.edu/news-article/maine-indian-education-posts-landmark-gains-attendance-and-achievement-superintendent Maine Department of Education, BARR 2026 State Handout (92 BARR schools, 11,250 students, 2,667 educators, vs 463 non-BARR schools; chronic absenteeism decline 14.6 points in BARR schools): https://www.maine.gov/doe/sites/maine.gov.doe/files/inline-files/BARR%20-%202026%20State%20Hadnout%20-%207.22.2026.pdf University of Southern Maine, Maine Education Policy Research Institute, 2026 report for policymakers (enrollment roughly 4% below pre-pandemic; chronic absenteeism 31% in 2021-22, 24% in 2023-24, 16% pre-pandemic): https://usm.maine.edu/cepare/wp-content/uploads/sites/481/2026/07/2026_June_MEPRI-Report_Implications-for-Policymakers_FINAL.pdf Brewer School Department, Chronic Absenteeism and Attendance Information (Maine compulsory attendance ages 7-17; absent if not present for more than 50% of the day; state reporting and truancy reporting to DHHS and law enforcement): https://www.breweredu.org/article/70421

Rhode Island districts are cutting staff and hunting for savings as energy, transportation, health care, and special education costs climb for fiscal 2027 — Cranston cut six point four million dollars including thirty paraprofessionals, Warwick reports special education costs up fourteen percent since fiscal 2024, and the funding formula review that might change the math will not report for nearly a year — plus Providence opens applications for two school board seats that begin in January.

item.title: [Tennessee] Education Daily — October 23, 2026: The Firm Behind the Takeover, a Retention Rebound That Isn't Finished, and a Shrinking Cohort
item.description:
Three Tennessee stories about capacity: Chalkbeat Tennessee reports that MGT, the Florida consulting firm that helped launch Houston's state takeover, has been drafting bylaws, contract rules, and an executive director job description for the Memphis-Shelby County oversight board since July — work the board accepted eight to one, funded by local philanthropy rather than the board itself; a Nashville Focal analysis of state data finds teacher retention has risen from its 2023-24 low but has not returned to earlier levels; and a Tennessee Firefly report on ExcelinEd data shows a shrinking young cohort — 83,021 births in 2023, kindergarten enrollment down five percent — pressing districts from Memphis, which closed five schools last year, to the growth counties of Middle Tennessee, nine days before every district's funding-formula accountability report is due to the state on November 1.
Sources: - Chalkbeat Tennessee (October 23, 2026) — reporting on MGT's work for the state-appointed Memphis-Shelby County Schools oversight board: bylaws, the $50,000 contract-approval process, the executive director job description, the 8-1 board vote, philanthropic funding via Seeding Success, and the proposed six months of support valued at $1 million — chalkbeat.org/tennessee; search MGT Memphis oversight board - Nashville Focal (October 23, 2026) — analysis of Tennessee state education data on teacher retention: risen from the 2023-24 low, not back to earlier levels — focalnews.org; search Tennessee teacher retention - Tennessee Firefly (October 22, 2026), reporting on an ExcelinEd report — 83,021 Tennessee births in 2023 (about 4% fewer than 2007), public kindergarten enrollment down 5% in 2024, district gains in Rutherford, Montgomery, Williamson, and Wilson counties and losses in Memphis-Shelby County — tennesseefirefly.com; search ExcelinEd Tennessee births enrollment - Tennessee Department of Education — Tennessee Investment in Student Achievement (TISA) district accountability reports due November 1 — tn.gov/education

item.title: [Utah] Education Daily — October 23, 2026: Thirteen Schools Under Study in a District That Has Not Opened Yet
item.description:
Utah's newest school district has not opened its doors yet, and it is already deciding which schools to close: the Timpanogos School District board voted unanimously this week to move sixth graders to junior high and ninth graders to high school for 2027-28, while thirteen schools — three junior highs and ten elementaries — sit under a closure study that points to a final decision in December, with elementary enrollment back at 1980 levels and three quarters of the district's elementary schools projected to fall outside its own size criteria by 2030.

item.title: [Wyoming] Education Daily — October 26, 2026: Midwest Fights for Its Upper Grades
item.description:
Tonight the Natrona County School District One trustees take up a proposal to end grades six through twelve at Midwest School in twenty twenty-seven to twenty twenty-eight, while kindergarten through fifth grade stays. The district's email to families calls the upper program significantly overstaffed and cites the changed state funding model, but no savings figure has been published. Midwest, the district's only preschool-through-twelfth-grade school with about one hundred twenty-seven students and a four-day week, answered with a town hall of more than one hundred people, a plea for time, charter and new-district alternatives, and a request at the state school facilities committee for a ninety-day stay.

item.title: The Right That Stops at the Schoolhouse Door
item.description:
Lock the door, pull the shade, move the children to the hard corner. The lockdown drill is rehearsed in every school in America — and it is the closest thing public school teachers have to a workplace safety law. In this national episode, Alex and Jordan trace why: a single definition in the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 wrote every public employee in the country out of the nation's workplace-safety law, and the right to a workplace free from recognized hazards stops at the schoolhouse door. We built the count from OSHA's own registry: in 29 of the 56 states, districts, and territories, a public school employee has a real safety regulator; in 27, there is no one to complain to. Plus the bargain police and firefighters got and teachers never did, the IDEA collision that stops abatement where a student is the hazard, New York's 2024 law that proves the fix can be built, and New Hampshire's paper right — a petition process aimed at a rulebook with no violence standard in it. The full written feature and the jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction coverage map are published with this story at educationacrossthestates.com.
Sources — OSHA, State Plans (22 full plans covering private and public sector workers; 7 public-sector-only plans: Connecticut, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, U.S. Virgin Islands): https://www.osha.gov/stateplans ; Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, section 3(5) definition of "employer" and section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/completeoshact and https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/section5-duties ; Littler, "New York Amends Workplace Violence Prevention Law to Extend Coverage to Public Schools" (Labor Law section 27-b, effective January 4, 2024): https://www.littler.com/news-analysis/asap/new-york-amends-workplace-violence-prevention-law-extend-coverage-public-schools ; Parker & Covert LLP on California SB 553 / Labor Code section 6401.9 (written workplace violence prevention plans, including school districts, by July 1, 2024): https://www.parkercovert.com/new-requirements-for-california-employers-to-implement-workplace-violence-prevention-plans-by-july-2024 ; New Hampshire RSA chapter 277 (277:13-a employee petition for inspection; 277:15-a post-incident inspections naming school districts): https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXIII/277/277-mrg.htm ; Individuals with Disabilities Education Act discipline provisions, 20 U.S.C. 1415(k): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/1415 ; Bricker & Eckler on Ohio's Public Employment Risk Reduction Program (PERRP, ORC chapter 4167): https://www.brickergraydon.com/insights/publications/PERRP-are-your-employees-safe

item.title: [Arkansas] Education Daily — October 27, 2026: The Conference After Removal

item.title: [NH] Nashua School Board Watch — Correction: Finance & Operations Committee, October 19, 2026
item.description:
MINUTES CORRECTION: The formal minutes for the October 19, 2026 Finance & Operations Committee are now posted, and this watch checked them against our corrected report on that meeting, as promised. Most of the reporting is confirmed exactly — all seven special education contract approvals passed 2-0 at the caps we reported (ACM Staffing $79,560, which also resolves the packet discrepancy we flagged; Beyond Words $46,800; Champion Speech Therapy $90,935; SLP Mama-to-be amendment to $76,930; Amergis $43,680; BlazerWorks $206,640; special education services $57,000 — $554,645 in new or expanded authority), the FY27 September Transfer Report was approved, and the solar power purchase agreements for Main Dunstable, Birch Hill, Bicentennial, and the School Administration Building were approved. One money item was materially different: we reported three CERF vehicles totaling $223,523, including a $56,296 Transit van; the minutes record approval of four purchases totaling $266,777.07 — dump truck $90,100, F-250 pickup $77,127, Maverick pickup $34,407, and a field tractor $65,143.07, with no Transit van. The minutes also record an information item we missed: a proposed joint city-school ERP system at approximately $9 million (no vote taken). Only two committee members were present, and every vote passed 2-0.
Also in this episode: the Board of Education did not meet on Monday, October 26 as previously listed — the full board meets Wednesday, October 28 at 5:00 PM to take up these recommendations (with the dump truck and Maverick amounts already revised in that agenda), followed by the Facilities Master Plan public hearing at 6:00 PM. Official documents confirm a board meeting on November 16 but do not label it the facilities vote; that timing is unconfirmed.
Watch board meetings live via the meeting link on nashua.edu under the Board of Education section.
Listener poll: https://strawpoll.com/xVg718Km6yr
Sources: - Nashua School District, Finance & Operations Committee Minutes, October 19, 2026 (2-page PDF, linked from the Finance and Operations page on nashua.edu): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1B1fUfvntA1NU-zFrUNd1kSDfVvEZaOf3/view?usp=drive_link - Nashua School District, Finance and Operations agendas and minutes page (nashua.edu > Our District > Board of Education > BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes > Finance and Operations): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-agendas-and-minutes/finance-and-operations - Nashua School District, Board of Education Meeting Agenda and Attachments, October 28, 2026 (164-page PDF, linked from the BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes page): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MmNdFQyC0MMlAfyvi-IxksfgvUNDZvUo/view?usp=drive_link - Nashua School District, BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes, October 2026 section (October 13 and October 19 minutes posted; no October 26 entry): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-agendas-and-minutes - Nashua Board of Education meeting schedule, October-November 2026 (nashua.edu; October 26 blank, October 28 BOE meeting 5 PM + public hearing 6 PM, November 16 BOE meeting 6 PM): https://www.nashua.edu/our-district/board-of-education/boe-meeting-schedule - Verification steps: open nashua.edu, choose Our District > Board of Education > BOE Meeting Agendas and Minutes > Finance and Operations, open the October 19, 2026 Minutes PDF, and compare each recorded 2-0 vote and dollar amount against this episode; then open the October 28, 2026 Agenda and Attachments PDF (Finance & Operations recommendations, pp. 1-2) to see the amounts the full board will vote on.

item.title: [American Samoa] Education Daily — October 27, 2026: When the Teacher Is Out — Who Teaches?
item.description:
When a teacher is absent in American Samoa, classes may be combined, covered by an adult without adequate preparation, or lose planned instructional time — and the Department of Education's emerging Substitute Teacher Equity Program Support, called Steps, is being built with the Pacific East Comprehensive Center to fix that, starting with discovery, a sustainable framework, and a focused pilot. Plus a contrast: the August deep-sea educator workshop that protected student learning by timing forty teachers' training before students returned.
Sources: - Pacific East Comprehensive Center, Improving Student Access to Learning Environments When Staffing Capacity is Strained in American Samoa — the Steps (S.T.E.P.S.) high-leverage problem, current fallbacks for uncovered absences, pilot support areas in instructional quality, student engagement, teacher support, and workforce development, and the discovery-to-pilot sequence: https://pacificeastcc.org/islands/improving-student-access-to-learning-environments-when-staffing-capacity-is-strained-in-american-samoa/ - NOAA Ocean Exploration, NOAA Ocean Exploration and Partners Host Deep-Sea Educator Workshop in American Samoa — August 19-20, 2026 workshop at the Tauese P.F. Sunia Ocean Center, forty educators from kindergarten through twelfth grade, live connection to NOAA Ship Okeanos Explorer, and supplies for four instructional kits: https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/news/noaa-ocean-exploration-and-partners-host-deep-sea-educator-workshop-in-american-samoa/ - American Samoa Department of Education homepage (system totals: more than 12,000 students in one territorial system) — search amsamoadoe.com for the ASDOE homepage
